lesson.grammar_point: used to + verb for past habits and states: affirmative, negative and questions

listenings.text: Hi, I'm Mike, from Ohio. In the nineties, I used to spend my Sunday evenings next to the radio. The station used to play the top forty, and I used to wait for my favorite songs with my finger on the record button. If the DJ talked over the beginning of the song, I used to get so angry! Then I used to make mixtapes for my friends, track by track. Once I made one for a girl I liked. It took me a whole weekend. Did it work? No, it didn't. Now I make playlists on my phone in two minutes. It's easier, but I don't think anybody will remember my playlists in thirty years.

I've worked on the radio in London for thirty years. When I started, listeners used to call the station or send a letter to ask for a song. Can you imagine? A letter! Bands used to wait months for their first single to play on the radio. Now a song can be a hit in one day, because millions of people stream it on their phones. Songs used to be longer, too. Today the chorus comes very early, because people skip quickly. But one thing surprises me. Young listeners know the old rock songs. Often they hear a cover first, and then they discover the original. Good songs always come back.

paras: Think about the eighties and the nineties. People used to wait for their favorite song on the radio, sometimes for an hour. Many teenagers used to record songs from the radio on a cassette, and they used to make a mix for a friend, track by track. When you bought an album, you used to listen to the whole thing, from the first song to the last, and you used to read the lyrics in the little book inside the CD.

Today, almost everybody streams music on a phone. You do not wait for anything: every song in the world is one click away. People make a playlist for every moment, for running, for working, for a long drive. Some experts say that many hits today are shorter than before, and that the catchy chorus comes much earlier in the song, because listeners skip a track very quickly.

But the old songs are still here. Old rock bands still fill stadiums, and young artists often record a cover of a song their parents used to love. Maybe we did not use to have so many choices, but we used to listen with more attention. The good news is that we can still do that: choose an album, press play, and do not skip.
